title: Product Sales Analysis III
statement:
One table records sales:

- `Sales(sale_id, product_id, year, quantity, price)`: each row is one sale of `product_id` in `year`, of `quantity` units at the per-unit `price`. The pair `(sale_id, year)` is unique. A product can have several sales in the same year, even identical-looking ones with different `sale_id`s.

For each product, its **first year** is the smallest `year` in which it has any sale. Report every sale that a product made in its first year, one output row per such sale (keep repeated rows; do not merge them). Output the columns `product_id`, `first_year` (that sale's year), `quantity` and `price`. Sales from later years are not reported. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: A product may have several sales in the same year
reference:
WITH first_years AS (
  SELECT product_id, MIN(year) AS first_year
  FROM Sales
  GROUP BY product_id
)
SELECT s.product_id, f.first_year, s.quantity, s.price
FROM Sales AS s
JOIN first_years AS f
  ON f.product_id = s.product_id
 AND f.first_year = s.year;
brute:
SELECT s.product_id, s.year AS first_year, s.quantity, s.price
FROM Sales AS s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM Sales AS earlier
  WHERE earlier.product_id = s.product_id
    AND earlier.year < s.year
)
notes:
## Intuition

Two facts are needed for each sale: which product it belongs to and whether its year is that product's earliest. The earliest year is a per-product aggregate, `MIN(year)` grouped by `product_id`, so it has to be computed first in its own stage. Joining it back to `Sales` on both the product and the year then keeps exactly the first-year sales, all of them, including repeats.

## Approach

1. `first_years`: group `Sales` by `product_id` and take `MIN(year)` as `first_year`.
2. Join every sale `s` to its product's row `f` in `first_years`, requiring `s.year = f.first_year` as part of the join condition.
3. Select `product_id`, `first_year`, `quantity` and `price` for each surviving sale.

## Example 1, step by step

- `first_years` holds `(100, 2008)` and `(200, 2011)`.
- Sale 1 (product 100, 2008) matches `(100, 2008)` and is kept as `100, 2008, 10, 5000`.
- Sale 2 (product 100, 2009) has the right product but year 2009 ≠ 2008, so it is dropped.
- Sale 7 (product 200, 2011) matches `(200, 2011)` and is kept as `200, 2011, 15, 9000`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(S) with hashing for S sales: one grouping pass to build `first_years` and one hash join back to `Sales`.
- Space: O(P) for the P rows of `first_years`, plus the output.

## Pitfalls

- `SELECT product_id, MIN(year), quantity, price ... GROUP BY product_id` returns one row per product with `quantity` and `price` from an arbitrary row (or is rejected under `ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY`), and loses extra first-year sales.
- Matching on the year alone (`WHERE year IN (SELECT MIN(year) ...)`) mixes products up; the match must use the product and the year together.
- `ROW_NUMBER()` per product keeps one sale even when the first year has several; `RANK()` or the join keeps them all. `DISTINCT` likewise wrongly merges identical sales.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `first_years` | one row per product: its earliest sale year as `first_year` |
| `s` | `Sales`, one row per sale |
| `f` | the `first_years` row of the sale's product |
| `ON ... AND f.first_year = s.year` | keeps only sales made in that first year |

narration.1: The first stage computes each product's earliest sale year.
narration.2: MIN(year) per product is that product's first year.
narration.4: One group per product, so first_years has one row per product.
narration.6: Report the product, its first year and the quantity and price of each kept sale.
narration.7: Start from every sale, since several sales can belong to the first year.
narration.8: Join each sale to its product's first-year row.
narration.10: Keep the sale only when its year equals the product's first year.
